Sign up for free Δ The state Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS§ionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=II) allows the Legislature to amend a ballot initiative without another vote if the initiative permits it. That’s a relatively common clause in ballot measures, and Prop. 40 includes it. Megan Jones, a tax attorney at Holland & Knight, said proponents’ claims that the tax could never be changed are disingenuous. “If it’s going to further the purposes, then they could,” Jones said. For example, voters passed the Political Reform Act, which governs campaign finance and lobbying rules, in 1974 and lawmakers have amended it almost continually since (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/the-law/the-political-reform-act/). Similarly, lawmakers have amended the Mental Health Services Act, a voter-approved 1% income tax on millionaires, 10 times since its passage in 2004. None of those amendments adjusted the tax rate. Most recently, lawmakers voted to substantially alter how the state spends mental health money and raise additional bond funds. Those changes went back to voters in 2024 as Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/). But there isn’t always a clear line for when voters need to approve changes, experts say. “It is common for the Legislature to make amendments,” Colantuono said. “It is (also) common for there to be disputes about those amendments.” ‘Furthers the purposes of’ “Ultimately, it ends up in court,” said Chris Parker, a principal tax attorney at the firm Baker Tilly. The California Supreme Court ruled in a 1995 case (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/11/1243.html) that the Legislature may amend voter-approved laws if the changes can be interpreted as furthering voters’ original goals “by any reasonable construction” — giving lawmakers broad latitude. In 2021, the state Supreme Court held that the Legislature appropriately amended Proposition 57 (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2021/s259011.html), a criminal justice reform measure, by barring the transferring of minors under 16 to adult court. Justices cited the 1995 case, noting that “a strong presumption of constitutionality supports the Legislature’s acts.” Still, the language of the proposition matters. A few years earlier, in 2019, the Third District Court of Appeal held that a legislative attempt to allow public funding of political campaigns (https://www4.courts.ca.gov/opinions/archive/C086334.PDF) “directly conflicts with a primary purpose” of the Political Reform Act. Lawmakers responded by passing a new bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) asking voters to weigh in directly — it appears on this year’s ballot as Proposition 4. Judges look at two things, Coluantuono said: what reasonable voters thought they were approving, and whether later legislative changes helped that goal, or got in the way. Certain provisions of Prop. 40 would make it difficult for lawmakers to expand the tax beyond billionaires. The 1995 case established that courts may weigh the language of a ballot measure, arguments printed in the voter guide, and historical context when deciding whether change is consistent with voter intent. Prop. 40’s purpose and intent section (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) says the measure is meant to support healthcare and education “by raising revenue from a one-time tax on billionaire wealth” — referencing billionaire wealth three times. The voter guide arguments similarly target “approximately 200 California billionaires.” “They could probably adjust the structure of the tax in marginal ways, but what they couldn’t do is make it a more than a one-time tax, and they probably couldn’t lower the threshold on wealth,” Coluantuono said. Opponents contend lawmakers could interpret the purpose of the act far more broadly, and a court would agree. They point to the first listed purpose of the initiative that says the tax is meant to “protect access to high quality, equitable health care, and to support funding for kindergarten through grade fourteen public education and food assistance programs.” Opponents also say the proposal gives the Legislature the authority to change all parts of the initiative, including the constitutional provisions. “Prop 40’s findings and statement of purpose and intent were carefully crafted to ensure that extending the tax to non-billionaires would be consistent with the measure,” said Kurt Oneto, a lawyer for the No on 40 campaign, in a statement. Experts said the question would likely come down to how a court read the act’s purposes. A separate concern: how do you prove wealth? Should Prop. 40 pass, it would create an entirely new tax structure in California — one that assigns a value to very wealthy people’s investments, public and private businesses, as well as personal property such as art or car collections. Valuing something like a tech startup that hasn’t produced a product or gone public could prove especially difficult, Parker said. “The excise tax that’s being proposed here is on potential,” he said. “The question then is, if we open the door to taxing potential, when does that stop?” Lawmakers have periodically tried to pass wealth taxes, but the bills quickly stalled. This marks the first time voters will directly decide on one, making Prop. 40 a crucial test of how much appetite Californians have for his kind of tax structure. Jones said the bigger worry isn’t the tax itself, but other taxes that could follow. “It’s a slippery slope,” she said. Coluantuono said it would still be politically risky for lawmakers to try to implement a wealth tax on everyday Californians, but history shows temporary taxes have more than once become permanent. “When we get a revenue stream in the government and we start spending it on services that people value… there’s tremendous political pressure to prevent the sunset,” he said. Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo IN SUMMARY Prop. 40 opponents say the billionaire tax allows lawmakers to change the measure with a two-thirds vote. They warn it opens the door to future wealth taxes on everyday Californians. This is only partially true. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Opponents of Proposition 40 have a message for voters: Don’t be fooled. The billionaire tax is a “Trojan horse” for new taxes on all Californians, ads proclaim (https://www.facebook.com/ads/library/?active_status=active&ad_type=all&country=US&id=1362825008785008&is_targeted_country=false&media_type=all&search_type=page&sort_data[mode]=total_impressions&sort_data[direction]=desc). But is that true? Tucked into the initiative is language granting the Legislature authority to amend the tax by a two-thirds vote “if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.” Opponents argue lawmakers and a future governor could, with the stroke of a pen, expand the wealth tax to people with far less than $1 billion. In a high-tax state, that argument could hold a lot of sway with voters. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put Prop. 40 on the ballot; the initiative would levy a one-time, 5% tax on billionaire’s assets. The union rejects the premise of the ad. It says the tax is limited to billionaires and any legislative amendment would have to hew closely to that purpose. Dave Regan, president of SEIU-UHW, said opponents’ ads are pure scare tactics. “The billionaire tax is a tax on billionaires. Period. If you’re not a billionaire, you don’t pay the tax,” Regan said in a statement to CalMatters. Rob Lapsley, president of the California Business Roundtable, the group that paid for the ad, said the message was meant to highlight the policy implications of a wealth tax and the power Prop. 40 gives lawmakers. “Californians deserve to understand those issues and what they could mean for taxpayers and the state’s economy,” Lapsley said in a statement. A separate, billionaire-backed group opposed to Prop. 40 has also said the initiative “gives politicians the power to expand the tax to anyone.” The truth lies somewhere in between. California courts have given lawmakers real authority to amend laws created by ballot initiatives if the original text of the initiative permits it. However, that power is not unlimited and the measure includes language restricting future legislative changes, said Michael Colantuono, an attorney with expertise in state election law. Opponents’ ads also don’t mention that Prop. 40 writes the tax into the state Constitution, not just state law, so expanding it would likely require another trip to the ballot. Legislative authority Legal experts agree that if Prop. 40 passes, lawmakers would be able to make certain amendments without taking it back to voters. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ The state Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS§ionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=II) allows the Legislature to amend a ballot initiative without another vote if the initiative permits it. That’s a relatively common clause in ballot measures, and Prop. 40 includes it. Megan Jones, a tax attorney at Holland & Knight, said proponents’ claims that the tax could never be changed are disingenuous. “If it’s going to further the purposes, then they could,” Jones said. For example, voters passed the Political Reform Act, which governs campaign finance and lobbying rules, in 1974 and lawmakers have amended it almost continually since (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/the-law/the-political-reform-act/). Similarly, lawmakers have amended the Mental Health Services Act, a voter-approved 1% income tax on millionaires, 10 times since its passage in 2004. None of those amendments adjusted the tax rate. Most recently, lawmakers voted to substantially alter how the state spends mental health money and raise additional bond funds. Those changes went back to voters in 2024 as Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/). But there isn’t always a clear line for when voters need to approve changes, experts say. “It is common for the Legislature to make amendments,” Colantuono said. “It is (also) common for there to be disputes about those amendments.” ‘Furthers the purposes of’ “Ultimately, it ends up in court,” said Chris Parker, a principal tax attorney at the firm Baker Tilly. The California Supreme Court ruled in a 1995 case (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/11/1243.html) that the Legislature may amend voter-approved laws if the changes can be interpreted as furthering voters’ original goals “by any reasonable construction” — giving lawmakers broad latitude. In 2021, the state Supreme Court held that the Legislature appropriately amended Proposition 57 (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2021/s259011.html), a criminal justice reform measure, by barring the transferring of minors under 16 to adult court. Justices cited the 1995 case, noting that “a strong presumption of constitutionality supports the Legislature’s acts.” Still, the language of the proposition matters. A few years earlier, in 2019, the Third District Court of Appeal held that a legislative attempt to allow public funding of political campaigns (https://www4.courts.ca.gov/opinions/archive/C086334.PDF) “directly conflicts with a primary purpose” of the Political Reform Act. Lawmakers responded by passing a new bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) asking voters to weigh in directly — it appears on this year’s ballot as Proposition 4. Judges look at two things, Coluantuono said: what reasonable voters thought they were approving, and whether later legislative changes helped that goal, or got in the way. Certain provisions of Prop. 40 would make it difficult for lawmakers to expand the tax beyond billionaires. The 1995 case established that courts may weigh the language of a ballot measure, arguments printed in the voter guide, and historical context when deciding whether change is consistent with voter intent. Prop. 40’s purpose and intent section (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) says the measure is meant to support healthcare and education “by raising revenue from a one-time tax on billionaire wealth” — referencing billionaire wealth three times. The voter guide arguments similarly target “approximately 200 California billionaires.” “They could probably adjust the structure of the tax in marginal ways, but what they couldn’t do is make it a more than a one-time tax, and they probably couldn’t lower the threshold on wealth,” Coluantuono said. Opponents contend lawmakers could interpret the purpose of the act far more broadly, and a court would agree. They point to the first listed purpose of the initiative that says the tax is meant to “protect access to high quality, equitable health care, and to support funding for kindergarten through grade fourteen public education and food assistance programs.” Opponents also say the proposal gives the Legislature the authority to change all parts of the initiative, including the constitutional provisions. “Prop 40’s findings and statement of purpose and intent were carefully crafted to ensure that extending the tax to non-billionaires would be consistent with the measure,” said Kurt Oneto, a lawyer for the No on 40 campaign, in a statement. Experts said the question would likely come down to how a court read the act’s purposes. A separate concern: how do you prove wealth? Should Prop. 40 pass, it would create an entirely new tax structure in California — one that assigns a value to very wealthy people’s investments, public and private businesses, as well as personal property such as art or car collections. Valuing something like a tech startup that hasn’t produced a product or gone public could prove especially difficult, Parker said. “The excise tax that’s being proposed here is on potential,” he said. “The question then is, if we open the door to taxing potential, when does that stop?” Lawmakers have periodically tried to pass wealth taxes, but the bills quickly stalled. This marks the first time voters will directly decide on one, making Prop. 40 a crucial test of how much appetite Californians have for his kind of tax structure. Jones said the bigger worry isn’t the tax itself, but other taxes that could follow. “It’s a slippery slope,” she said. Coluantuono said it would still be politically risky for lawmakers to try to implement a wealth tax on everyday Californians, but history shows temporary taxes have more than once become permanent. “When we get a revenue stream in the government and we start spending it on services that people value… there’s tremendous political pressure to prevent the sunset,” he said. Endorsement: Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what Prop 42 asks you to believe
Prop 42 is the second of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
Is California coming for your retirement account?
That’s what the backers of Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot would have you believe. Their measure would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — such as stocks and retirement accounts (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop42-110326.pdf) — and other forms of asset ownership, while also banning certain retroactive state taxes.
Evan McLaughlin, political director for the California Professional Firefighters, which represents firefighter unions across the state, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview that Prop 42 adds important protections for working families. In recent years, Democratic state lawmakers have introduced a handful of wealth tax proposals targeting the rich. But once you take the lid off a new form of taxation, he argued, there’s nothing stopping it from spreading to the rest of us.
“The Legislature isn’t going to wall themselves off from doing this,” McLaughlin said. “We think that it’s a public benefit to people to say, ‘If you’re going to try to tax these types of retirement assets and 401(k)s and personal savings, you need to go to a vote of the people.’”

That certainly sounds reasonable. But no one is coming for your 401(k).
California largely follows (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17501) the federal government’s framework for evaluating pensions and retirement accounts — taxing funds when they’re withdrawn, not when they’re deposited — and there are no concerted efforts to change that.
In reality, Prop 42 is just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
The measure is backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php). And it explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 42 (or its cousin Prop 41 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)) passes with more votes.

It’s true Prop 40 does add a potentially concerning new wrinkle by including Roth IRAs and “substantially similar” accounts worth more than $10 million in its formula for taxable wealth. David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and one of Prop 42’s opponents, pointed to a ProPublica investigation (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) that found Peter Thiel and other billionaires have quietly used Roth IRAs to amass gargantuan tax-exempt fortunes.
But Prop 40 specifically excludes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) qualified pensions and retirement accounts (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:26+section:219+edition:prelim)#:~:text=(5)%20Active%20participant), including 401(k)s, from being considered as “assets.”
There is little merit in adding yet another ballot-box budgeting rule to California’s already head-spinning list of restrictions. Lawmakers have already killed all six wealth tax proposals introduced since 2019; none made it out of their house of origin, and some didn’t even get a hearing (https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2021/04/alex-lee-progressive-california/).
Meanwhile, Prop 42’s ban on retroactive state taxes — which includes an exemption for natural and fiscal emergencies — is also unnecessary and could create legal complications.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 1993 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-512/pdf/USREPORTS-512-26.pdf) that retroactive taxes can be constitutional if “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational means.” The court determined the retroactive tax in question, which was “only slightly longer than one year,” was “modest” and met the standard.

Yet Prop 42 outlaws any tax approved by the Legislature that applies more than one year retroactively — raising questions about how the measure might intersect with the standard set by the nation’s highest court.
Its true target is Prop 40, which would tax any billionaire living in California as of Jan. 1, 2026. And you don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
If you disagree with Prop 40, you can simply vote no.

Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo IN SUMMARY Prop. 40 opponents say the billionaire tax allows lawmakers to change the measure with a two-thirds vote. They warn it opens the door to future wealth taxes on everyday Californians. This is only partially true. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Opponents of Proposition 40 have a message for voters: Don’t be fooled. The billionaire tax is a “Trojan horse” for new taxes on all Californians, ads proclaim (https://www.facebook.com/ads/library/?active_status=active&ad_type=all&country=US&id=1362825008785008&is_targeted_country=false&media_type=all&search_type=page&sort_data[mode]=total_impressions&sort_data[direction]=desc). But is that true? Tucked into the initiative is language granting the Legislature authority to amend the tax by a two-thirds vote “if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.” Opponents argue lawmakers and a future governor could, with the stroke of a pen, expand the wealth tax to people with far less than $1 billion. In a high-tax state, that argument could hold a lot of sway with voters. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put Prop. 40 on the ballot; the initiative would levy a one-time, 5% tax on billionaire’s assets. The union rejects the premise of the ad. It says the tax is limited to billionaires and any legislative amendment would have to hew closely to that purpose. Dave Regan, president of SEIU-UHW, said opponents’ ads are pure scare tactics. “The billionaire tax is a tax on billionaires. Period. If you’re not a billionaire, you don’t pay the tax,” Regan said in a statement to CalMatters. Rob Lapsley, president of the California Business Roundtable, the group that paid for the ad, said the message was meant to highlight the policy implications of a wealth tax and the power Prop. 40 gives lawmakers. “Californians deserve to understand those issues and what they could mean for taxpayers and the state’s economy,” Lapsley said in a statement. A separate, billionaire-backed group opposed to Prop. 40 has also said the initiative “gives politicians the power to expand the tax to anyone.” The truth lies somewhere in between. California courts have given lawmakers real authority to amend laws created by ballot initiatives if the original text of the initiative permits it. However, that power is not unlimited and the measure includes language restricting future legislative changes, said Michael Colantuono, an attorney with expertise in state election law. Opponents’ ads also don’t mention that Prop. 40 writes the tax into the state Constitution, not just state law, so expanding it would likely require another trip to the ballot. Legislative authority Legal experts agree that if Prop. 40 passes, lawmakers would be able to make certain amendments without taking it back to voters. Sign up for free Δ The state Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS§ionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=II) allows the Legislature to amend a ballot initiative without another vote if the initiative permits it. That’s a relatively common clause in ballot measures, and Prop. 40 includes it. Megan Jones, a tax attorney at Holland & Knight, said proponents’ claims that the tax could never be changed are disingenuous. “If it’s going to further the purposes, then they could,” Jones said. For example, voters passed the Political Reform Act, which governs campaign finance and lobbying rules, in 1974 and lawmakers have amended it almost continually since (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/the-law/the-political-reform-act/). Similarly, lawmakers have amended the Mental Health Services Act, a voter-approved 1% income tax on millionaires, 10 times since its passage in 2004. None of those amendments adjusted the tax rate. Most recently, lawmakers voted to substantially alter how the state spends mental health money and raise additional bond funds. Those changes went back to voters in 2024 as Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/). But there isn’t always a clear line for when voters need to approve changes, experts say. “It is common for the Legislature to make amendments,” Colantuono said. “It is (also) common for there to be disputes about those amendments.” ‘Furthers the purposes of’ “Ultimately, it ends up in court,” said Chris Parker, a principal tax attorney at the firm Baker Tilly. The California Supreme Court ruled in a 1995 case (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/11/1243.html) that the Legislature may amend voter-approved laws if the changes can be interpreted as furthering voters’ original goals “by any reasonable construction” — giving lawmakers broad latitude. In 2021, the state Supreme Court held that the Legislature appropriately amended Proposition 57 (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2021/s259011.html), a criminal justice reform measure, by barring the transferring of minors under 16 to adult court. Justices cited the 1995 case, noting that “a strong presumption of constitutionality supports the Legislature’s acts.” Still, the language of the proposition matters. A few years earlier, in 2019, the Third District Court of Appeal held that a legislative attempt to allow public funding of political campaigns (https://www4.courts.ca.gov/opinions/archive/C086334.PDF) “directly conflicts with a primary purpose” of the Political Reform Act. Lawmakers responded by passing a new bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) asking voters to weigh in directly — it appears on this year’s ballot as Proposition 4. Judges look at two things, Coluantuono said: what reasonable voters thought they were approving, and whether later legislative changes helped that goal, or got in the way. Certain provisions of Prop. 40 would make it difficult for lawmakers to expand the tax beyond billionaires. The 1995 case established that courts may weigh the language of a ballot measure, arguments printed in the voter guide, and historical context when deciding whether change is consistent with voter intent. Prop. 40’s purpose and intent section (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) says the measure is meant to support healthcare and education “by raising revenue from a one-time tax on billionaire wealth” — referencing billionaire wealth three times. The voter guide arguments similarly target “approximately 200 California billionaires.” “They could probably adjust the structure of the tax in marginal ways, but what they couldn’t do is make it a more than a one-time tax, and they probably couldn’t lower the threshold on wealth,” Coluantuono said. Opponents contend lawmakers could interpret the purpose of the act far more broadly, and a court would agree. They point to the first listed purpose of the initiative that says the tax is meant to “protect access to high quality, equitable health care, and to support funding for kindergarten through grade fourteen public education and food assistance programs.” Opponents also say the proposal gives the Legislature the authority to change all parts of the initiative, including the constitutional provisions. “Prop 40’s findings and statement of purpose and intent were carefully crafted to ensure that extending the tax to non-billionaires would be consistent with the measure,” said Kurt Oneto, a lawyer for the No on 40 campaign, in a statement. Experts said the question would likely come down to how a court read the act’s purposes. A separate concern: how do you prove wealth? Should Prop. 40 pass, it would create an entirely new tax structure in California — one that assigns a value to very wealthy people’s investments, public and private businesses, as well as personal property such as art or car collections. Valuing something like a tech startup that hasn’t produced a product or gone public could prove especially difficult, Parker said. “The excise tax that’s being proposed here is on potential,” he said. “The question then is, if we open the door to taxing potential, when does that stop?” Lawmakers have periodically tried to pass wealth taxes, but the bills quickly stalled. This marks the first time voters will directly decide on one, making Prop. 40 a crucial test of how much appetite Californians have for his kind of tax structure. Jones said the bigger worry isn’t the tax itself, but other taxes that could follow. “It’s a slippery slope,” she said. Coluantuono said it would still be politically risky for lawmakers to try to implement a wealth tax on everyday Californians, but history shows temporary taxes have more than once become permanent. “When we get a revenue stream in the government and we start spending it on services that people value… there’s tremendous political pressure to prevent the sunset,” he said. Proposition 3
Make income taxes on higher earners permanent to fund education and healthcare
The tax, first enacted in 2012, is set to expire in 2031. Under the measure, income taxes for top earners range from 10.3% (for individual income over $360,000) to 12.3% (for individual income over $721,000), with graduated rates in between. Eighty-nine percent of the money goes to K-12 public schools and 11% goes to community colleges, with any excess going to public healthcare. The tax typically raises $5 billion to $15 billion a year — about 3% to 10% of overall K-12 spending. The California Teachers Association put this measure on the ballot.

Summary
Support
The tax has been a vital source of revenue for schools. Supporters say if Prop. 3 fails, the loss of up to $15 billion a year for schools will likely lead to layoffs, program cuts and other reductions.
Oppose
Opponents point out that California already has some of the highest income taxes in the country. They say the measure may spur wealthy Californians to leave for lower-tax states, taking jobs and revenue with them.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

By The Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)

The most hotly debated initiative on the November ballot is Proposition 40, which would impose a 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires. As this Editorial Board opined (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/13/endorsement-no-on-proposition-40s-reckless-wealth-tax/) in our opposition, the union-created Billionaire Tax Act would send a dangerous message to current and future entrepreneurs, and “have a chilling effect on investment.”
But two closely related measures, Propositions 41 and 42 (https://www.bakersfield.com/opinion/our-view/our-view-vote-no-on-propositions-40-41-42-tax-propositions-hurt-state-californians/article_1c8492b8-5fb9-4897-9f1c-c9ba56460e0d.amp.html) , have received much less attention — partly because they’re so complicated. By adding related measures to the ballot, opponents of Prop. 40 are hoping that voters approve one of these alternatives that will derail Prop. 40. Because these two measures have elements that contradict Prop. 40, the one that gets the highest vote totals (if voters OK them all) would go into effect.
Adding similar-sounding measures also muddies the waters, thus increasing the likelihood that confused voters vote “no” on all of them — thus accomplishing the main goal of stopping the billionaires’ tax. But our goal isn’t to map out political strategies (https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/nash-game/) . It’s a worthy effort to try to stop a disastrous new tax scheme.
Besides their intended purpose of blocking Prop. 40, the measures could protect taxpayers for years to come.
Specifically, Prop. 41 would require one-time audits of programs that any proposed special taxes would fund. Those audits, which must be completed before the initiative appears on the ballot, would be required to identify ways that such programs could cut annual costs by 10%, per an analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026) from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
While Prop. 40 exempts itself from state spending limits, Prop. 41 also requires new special-tax revenues to count toward the Gann Limit (https://www.sheehystrategygroup.com/news/2026/3/9/californias-state-appropriations-limit-gann-limit) — the 1979 constitutional amendment that caps the revenue the state can spend each year. The state has passed a number of workarounds over the years, but applying new revenues to this formula would potentially require the return of certain additional tax revenues to taxpayers (https://www.yesonprop41.org/about-prop41) and the earmarking of revenues to infrastructure.
Prop. 42 is more straightforward. Per theLAO (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=42&year=2026), the initiative prohibits “new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.” California doesn’t currently tax the ownership of financial assets and only taxes personal property in a limited way (e.g., vehicle license fees), but the measure’s passage “could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes.” It also limits imposition of retroactive taxes.
So would the Editorial Board support these measures even if they were standalone initiatives? The answers are unequivocal: Yes and yes.

Proposition 3
Make income taxes on higher earners permanent to fund education and healthcare
The tax, first enacted in 2012, is set to expire in 2031. Under the measure, income taxes for top earners range from 10.3% (for individual income over $360,000) to 12.3% (for individual income over $721,000), with graduated rates in between. Eighty-nine percent of the money goes to K-12 public schools and 11% goes to community colleges, with any excess going to public healthcare. The tax typically raises $5 billion to $15 billion a year — about 3% to 10% of overall K-12 spending. The California Teachers Association put this measure on the ballot.

These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. By The Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: September 21, 2026 at 2:39 PM PDT | UPDATED: September 21, 2026 at 2:56 PM PDT

The most hotly debated initiative on the November ballot is Proposition 40, which would impose a 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires. As this Editorial Board opined (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/13/endorsement-no-on-proposition-40s-reckless-wealth-tax/) in our opposition, the union-created Billionaire Tax Act would send a dangerous message to current and future entrepreneurs, and “have a chilling effect on investment.”
But two closely related measures, Propositions 41 and 42 (https://www.bakersfield.com/opinion/our-view/our-view-vote-no-on-propositions-40-41-42-tax-propositions-hurt-state-californians/article_1c8492b8-5fb9-4897-9f1c-c9ba56460e0d.amp.html) , have received much less attention — partly because they’re so complicated. By adding related measures to the ballot, opponents of Prop. 40 are hoping that voters approve one of these alternatives that will derail Prop. 40. Because these two measures have elements that contradict Prop. 40, the one that gets the highest vote totals (if voters OK them all) would go into effect.
Adding similar-sounding measures also muddies the waters, thus increasing the likelihood that confused voters vote “no” on all of them — thus accomplishing the main goal of stopping the billionaires’ tax. But our goal isn’t to map out political strategies (https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/nash-game/) . It’s a worthy effort to try to stop a disastrous new tax scheme.
Besides their intended purpose of blocking Prop. 40, the measures could protect taxpayers for years to come.
Specifically, Prop. 41 would require one-time audits of programs that any proposed special taxes would fund. Those audits, which must be completed before the initiative appears on the ballot, would be required to identify ways that such programs could cut annual costs by 10%, per an analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026) from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
While Prop. 40 exempts itself from state spending limits, Prop. 41 also requires new special-tax revenues to count toward the Gann Limit (https://www.sheehystrategygroup.com/news/2026/3/9/californias-state-appropriations-limit-gann-limit) — the 1979 constitutional amendment that caps the revenue the state can spend each year. The state has passed a number of workarounds over the years, but applying new revenues to this formula would potentially require the return of certain additional tax revenues to taxpayers (https://www.yesonprop41.org/about-prop41) and the earmarking of revenues to infrastructure.
Prop. 42 is more straightforward. Per theLAO (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=42&year=2026), the initiative prohibits “new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.” California doesn’t currently tax the ownership of financial assets and only taxes personal property in a limited way (e.g., vehicle license fees), but the measure’s passage “could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes.” It also limits imposition of retroactive taxes.
So would the Editorial Board support these measures even if they were standalone initiatives? The answers are unequivocal: Yes and yes.

The most hotly debated initiative on the November ballot is Proposition 40, which would impose a 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires. As this Editorial Board opined (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/13/endorsement-no-on-proposition-40s-reckless-wealth-tax/) in our opposition, the union-created Billionaire Tax Act would send a dangerous message to current and future entrepreneurs, and “have a chilling effect on investment.”
But two closely related measures, Propositions 41 and 42 (https://www.bakersfield.com/opinion/our-view/our-view-vote-no-on-propositions-40-41-42-tax-propositions-hurt-state-californians/article_1c8492b8-5fb9-4897-9f1c-c9ba56460e0d.amp.html) , have received much less attention — partly because they’re so complicated. By adding related measures to the ballot, opponents of Prop. 40 are hoping that voters approve one of these alternatives that will derail Prop. 40. Because these two measures have elements that contradict Prop. 40, the one that gets the highest vote totals (if voters OK them all) would go into effect.
Adding similar-sounding measures also muddies the waters, thus increasing the likelihood that confused voters vote “no” on all of them — thus accomplishing the main goal of stopping the billionaires’ tax. But our goal isn’t to map out political strategies (https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/nash-game/) . It’s a worthy effort to try to stop a disastrous new tax scheme.
Besides their intended purpose of blocking Prop. 40, the measures could protect taxpayers for years to come.
Specifically, Prop. 41 would require one-time audits of programs that any proposed special taxes would fund. Those audits, which must be completed before the initiative appears on the ballot, would be required to identify ways that such programs could cut annual costs by 10%, per an analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026) from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
While Prop. 40 exempts itself from state spending limits, Prop. 41 also requires new special-tax revenues to count toward the Gann Limit (https://www.sheehystrategygroup.com/news/2026/3/9/californias-state-appropriations-limit-gann-limit) — the 1979 constitutional amendment that caps the revenue the state can spend each year. The state has passed a number of workarounds over the years, but applying new revenues to this formula would potentially require the return of certain additional tax revenues to taxpayers (https://www.yesonprop41.org/about-prop41) and the earmarking of revenues to infrastructure.
Prop. 42 is more straightforward. Per theLAO (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=42&year=2026), the initiative prohibits “new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.” California doesn’t currently tax the ownership of financial assets and only taxes personal property in a limited way (e.g., vehicle license fees), but the measure’s passage “could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes.” It also limits imposition of retroactive taxes.
So would the Editorial Board support these measures even if they were standalone initiatives? The answers are unequivocal: Yes and yes.

Proposition 3
Make income taxes on higher earners permanent to fund education and healthcare
The tax, first enacted in 2012, is set to expire in 2031. Under the measure, income taxes for top earners range from 10.3% (for individual income over $360,000) to 12.3% (for individual income over $721,000), with graduated rates in between. Eighty-nine percent of the money goes to K-12 public schools and 11% goes to community colleges, with any excess going to public healthcare. The tax typically raises $5 billion to $15 billion a year — about 3% to 10% of overall K-12 spending. The California Teachers Association put this measure on the ballot.

The tax has been a vital source of revenue for schools. Supporters say if Prop. 3 fails, the loss of up to $15 billion a year for schools will likely lead to layoffs, program cuts and other reductions.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Outside spending
Separate from proposition committees, outside groups can pay for ads, mailers and other efforts to influence voters. They can’t coordinate that spending with proposition committees. There is no limit on how much they can spend.

PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT. Makes permanent existing voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 (adjusted annually for inflation). Allocates tax revenues to public education. By The Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)

The most hotly debated initiative on the November ballot is Proposition 40, which would impose a 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires. As this Editorial Board opined (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/13/endorsement-no-on-proposition-40s-reckless-wealth-tax/) in our opposition, the union-created Billionaire Tax Act would send a dangerous message to current and future entrepreneurs, and “have a chilling effect on investment.”
But two closely related measures, Propositions 41 and 42 (https://www.bakersfield.com/opinion/our-view/our-view-vote-no-on-propositions-40-41-42-tax-propositions-hurt-state-californians/article_1c8492b8-5fb9-4897-9f1c-c9ba56460e0d.amp.html) , have received much less attention — partly because they’re so complicated. By adding related measures to the ballot, opponents of Prop. 40 are hoping that voters approve one of these alternatives that will derail Prop. 40. Because these two measures have elements that contradict Prop. 40, the one that gets the highest vote totals (if voters OK them all) would go into effect.
Adding similar-sounding measures also muddies the waters, thus increasing the likelihood that confused voters vote “no” on all of them — thus accomplishing the main goal of stopping the billionaires’ tax. But our goal isn’t to map out political strategies (https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/nash-game/) . It’s a worthy effort to try to stop a disastrous new tax scheme.
Besides their intended purpose of blocking Prop. 40, the measures could protect taxpayers for years to come.
Specifically, Prop. 41 would require one-time audits of programs that any proposed special taxes would fund. Those audits, which must be completed before the initiative appears on the ballot, would be required to identify ways that such programs could cut annual costs by 10%, per an analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026) from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
While Prop. 40 exempts itself from state spending limits, Prop. 41 also requires new special-tax revenues to count toward the Gann Limit (https://www.sheehystrategygroup.com/news/2026/3/9/californias-state-appropriations-limit-gann-limit) — the 1979 constitutional amendment that caps the revenue the state can spend each year. The state has passed a number of workarounds over the years, but applying new revenues to this formula would potentially require the return of certain additional tax revenues to taxpayers (https://www.yesonprop41.org/about-prop41) and the earmarking of revenues to infrastructure.
Prop. 42 is more straightforward. Per theLAO (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=42&year=2026), the initiative prohibits “new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.” California doesn’t currently tax the ownership of financial assets and only taxes personal property in a limited way (e.g., vehicle license fees), but the measure’s passage “could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes.” It also limits imposition of retroactive taxes.
So would the Editorial Board support these measures even if they were standalone initiatives? The answers are unequivocal: Yes and yes.

Blog Post · October 9, 2026
How Can Californians Make Sense of the Tax Measures on the November Ballot?
Mary Severance (https://www.ppic.org/person/mary-severance/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
View Larger (javascript:void(0))
Mary Severance (https://www.ppic.org/person/mary-severance/)
Mary Severance (https://www.ppic.org/person/mary-severance/)
Five of the fourteen statewide initiatives on the November ballot are tax measures. What implications might these initiatives have, and how are voters feeling about them? These questions were the focus of a lunchtime discussion last week in Sacramento.
Mark Baldassare, director of the PPIC Statewide Survey, kicked off the event with key insights from the most recent survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/).
The bottom line on the tax measures? “California voters are giving the five tax measures mixed reviews. Four of the five have majority support—but they’re not big majorities; they’re not over 60%. So the outcome is very uncertain.”
Baldassare pointed to other survey findings that could factor into ballot choices. “Most Californians say that there are too many initiatives on the ballot, and that the ballot initiatives are confusing,” he said. “The default is to vote no if you’re unsure.”
More broadly still, Baldassare noted that Californians are feeling negative about where things are heading in the state and the nation: “Majorities expect bad economic times over the next 12 months, and there are low approval ratings for elected leaders and low trust in the federal and state governments.”
Baldassare’s briefing set the stage for a discussion between Tani Cantil-Sakauye, PPIC president and CEO; Gale Kaufman, president of Kaufman Strategies; and Rob Stutzman, founder and president of Stutzman Public Affairs.
Cantil-Sakauye asked the panelists about how the overall mood might affect election outcomes. “It’s as bad as I can remember in terms of the negativity,” said Kaufman. However, she added that if past experience holds, voters will do their research on each of the ballot measures. “They pick each one individually,” she said. “You can’t make a blanket statement.”
Stutzman noted that voter negativity extends to both parties. “As much as you’re hearing about the midterms dynamic being driven by how unpopular the president is,” he said, “you still have a very unpopular Democratic Party.”
The tax measure that has attracted the most voter interest so far is Proposition 40, the so-called billionaire’s tax. Stutzman noted that the strongest argument for Prop 40 is that too much wealth has been accumulated by too few people. But Kaufman said that the measure has been divisive: “The Yes side of 40 has fragmented the Democratic coalition of activists throughout the state.” As Stutzman pointed out, disagreement about the potential impact of Prop 40 “allows the No campaign to point out that Becerra, Hilton, and Newsom are all opposed . . . and say this must be a bad idea.”
While Proposition 3—which would extend a temporary marginal tax on high-income Californians—had majority support in PPIC’s September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), less than half of voters say they would vote yes on Proposition 43, which would raise the vote threshold for approving local taxes to two-thirds.
For Stutzman, the relative lack of support for Prop 43 was a bit unexpected: “I was a little surprised when I saw the numbers,” he said. “But I also know that the would-be Yes side is preparing to spend money to push this over the top.” Kaufman said she was not surprised. “Making it more difficult for local entities to be able to tax themselves,” she said, “has a huge impact on cities, counties and special districts, who are really in trouble.”
In the end, the panelists agreed that the sheer number of measures on the ballot could play a role in the outcome. “With 14 measures on the ballot,” said Kaufman, “I think there’s going to be tremendous confusion.”
***

Chris Hannan
# Taxing wealth is a dangerous step toward taxing retirement savings
...
By Chris HannanGuest contributor
Oct. 29, 2026 4:13 PM PT
...
- 3 min
...
I started my career as an apprentice sprinkler fitter, following my father into UA Local 709.
Today I lead the State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, representing nearly half a million workers who build and maintain our communities.
...
This November, Californians have an opportunity to protect the hard-earned retirement savings they have earned.
For the workers I represent, retirement isn’t a windfall.
It’s earned across jobsites from thousands of hours worked, over decades of early mornings, long shifts and hard physical work.

Blog Post · October 9, 2026
How Can Californians Make Sense of the Tax Measures on the November Ballot?
Mary Severance (https://www.ppic.org/person/mary-severance/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
View Larger (javascript:void(0))
Mary Severance (https://www.ppic.org/person/mary-severance/)
Mary Severance (https://www.ppic.org/person/mary-severance/)
Five of the fourteen statewide initiatives on the November ballot are tax measures. What implications might these initiatives have, and how are voters feeling about them? These questions were the focus of a lunchtime discussion last week in Sacramento.
Mark Baldassare, director of the PPIC Statewide Survey, kicked off the event with key insights from the most recent survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/).
The bottom line on the tax measures? “California voters are giving the five tax measures mixed reviews. Four of the five have majority support—but they’re not big majorities; they’re not over 60%. So the outcome is very uncertain.”
Baldassare pointed to other survey findings that could factor into ballot choices. “Most Californians say that there are too many initiatives on the ballot, and that the ballot initiatives are confusing,” he said. “The default is to vote no if you’re unsure.”
More broadly still, Baldassare noted that Californians are feeling negative about where things are heading in the state and the nation: “Majorities expect bad economic times over the next 12 months, and there are low approval ratings for elected leaders and low trust in the federal and state governments.”
Baldassare’s briefing set the stage for a discussion between Tani Cantil-Sakauye, PPIC president and CEO; Gale Kaufman, president of Kaufman Strategies; and Rob Stutzman, founder and president of Stutzman Public Affairs.
Cantil-Sakauye asked the panelists about how the overall mood might affect election outcomes. “It’s as bad as I can remember in terms of the negativity,” said Kaufman. However, she added that if past experience holds, voters will do their research on each of the ballot measures. “They pick each one individually,” she said. “You can’t make a blanket statement.”
Stutzman noted that voter negativity extends to both parties. “As much as you’re hearing about the midterms dynamic being driven by how unpopular the president is,” he said, “you still have a very unpopular Democratic Party.”
The tax measure that has attracted the most voter interest so far is Proposition 40, the so-called billionaire’s tax. Stutzman noted that the strongest argument for Prop 40 is that too much wealth has been accumulated by too few people. But Kaufman said that the measure has been divisive: “The Yes side of 40 has fragmented the Democratic coalition of activists throughout the state.” As Stutzman pointed out, disagreement about the potential impact of Prop 40 “allows the No campaign to point out that Becerra, Hilton, and Newsom are all opposed . . . and say this must be a bad idea.”
While Proposition 3—which would extend a temporary marginal tax on high-income Californians—had majority support in PPIC’s September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), less than half of voters say they would vote yes on Proposition 43, which would raise the vote threshold for approving local taxes to two-thirds.
For Stutzman, the relative lack of support for Prop 43 was a bit unexpected: “I was a little surprised when I saw the numbers,” he said. “But I also know that the would-be Yes side is preparing to spend money to push this over the top.” Kaufman said she was not surprised. “Making it more difficult for local entities to be able to tax themselves,” she said, “has a huge impact on cities, counties and special districts, who are really in trouble.”
In the end, the panelists agreed that the sheer number of measures on the ballot could play a role in the outcome. “With 14 measures on the ballot,” said Kaufman, “I think there’s going to be tremendous confusion.”
***

In the end, the panelists agreed that the sheer number of measures on the ballot could play a role in the outcome. “With 14 measures on the ballot,” said Kaufman, “I think there’s going to be tremendous confusion.”

How Can Californians Make Sense of the Tax Measures on the November Ballot?
Mary Severance (https://www.ppic.org/person/mary-severance/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
View Larger (javascript:void(0))
Mary Severance (https://www.ppic.org/person/mary-severance/)
Mary Severance (https://www.ppic.org/person/mary-severance/)
Five of the fourteen statewide initiatives on the November ballot are tax measures. What implications might these initiatives have, and how are voters feeling about them? These questions were the focus of a lunchtime discussion last week in Sacramento.
Mark Baldassare, director of the PPIC Statewide Survey, kicked off the event with key insights from the most recent survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/).
The bottom line on the tax measures? “California voters are giving the five tax measures mixed reviews. Four of the five have majority support—but they’re not big majorities; they’re not over 60%. So the outcome is very uncertain.”
Baldassare pointed to other survey findings that could factor into ballot choices. “Most Californians say that there are too many initiatives on the ballot, and that the ballot initiatives are confusing,” he said. “The default is to vote no if you’re unsure.”
More broadly still, Baldassare noted that Californians are feeling negative about where things are heading in the state and the nation: “Majorities expect bad economic times over the next 12 months, and there are low approval ratings for elected leaders and low trust in the federal and state governments.”
Baldassare’s briefing set the stage for a discussion between Tani Cantil-Sakauye, PPIC president and CEO; Gale Kaufman, president of Kaufman Strategies; and Rob Stutzman, founder and president of Stutzman Public Affairs.
Cantil-Sakauye asked the panelists about how the overall mood might affect election outcomes. “It’s as bad as I can remember in terms of the negativity,” said Kaufman. However, she added that if past experience holds, voters will do their research on each of the ballot measures. “They pick each one individually,” she said. “You can’t make a blanket statement.”
Stutzman noted that voter negativity extends to both parties. “As much as you’re hearing about the midterms dynamic being driven by how unpopular the president is,” he said, “you still have a very unpopular Democratic Party.”
The tax measure that has attracted the most voter interest so far is Proposition 40, the so-called billionaire’s tax. Stutzman noted that the strongest argument for Prop 40 is that too much wealth has been accumulated by too few people. But Kaufman said that the measure has been divisive: “The Yes side of 40 has fragmented the Democratic coalition of activists throughout the state.” As Stutzman pointed out, disagreement about the potential impact of Prop 40 “allows the No campaign to point out that Becerra, Hilton, and Newsom are all opposed . . . and say this must be a bad idea.”
While Proposition 3—which would extend a temporary marginal tax on high-income Californians—had majority support in PPIC’s September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), less than half of voters say they would vote yes on Proposition 43, which would raise the vote threshold for approving local taxes to two-thirds.
For Stutzman, the relative lack of support for Prop 43 was a bit unexpected: “I was a little surprised when I saw the numbers,” he said. “But I also know that the would-be Yes side is preparing to spend money to push this over the top.” Kaufman said she was not surprised. “Making it more difficult for local entities to be able to tax themselves,” she said, “has a huge impact on cities, counties and special districts, who are really in trouble.”
In the end, the panelists agreed that the sheer number of measures on the ballot could play a role in the outcome. “With 14 measures on the ballot,” said Kaufman, “I think there’s going to be tremendous confusion.”

Now I have a good picture. Notably even the LA Times columnist George Skelton says No on 41 & 42 ("Twin poison pills... deceptive games-playing"). The LA Times editorial board position? Let me check whether the LA Times endorsed on Prop 42. The CalMatters page listed media endorsements: Support — San Diego Union-Tribune, OC Register. Oppose — Sacramento Bee, SF Chronicle, Mercury News. LA Times not listed; Skelton (columnist) said No.

Let me check the LA Times editorial board endorsement list to see whether they took a position. Also check the League of Women Voters position on Prop 42 specifically, and California Democratic Party (opposed).

Additionally, let's check any legal analyses suggesting Prop 42 could have unintended consequences beyond wealth taxes — e.g., could it block a future tax on "personal belongings" like a boat tax or a tax on firearms? Also could it prevent the state from complying with certain federal requirements? Probably not.

Also consider the possibility that Prop 42 might conflict with Prop 41 or others. SF Chronicle said Props 41 and 42 do not conflict with each other.

Another key point: if a voter opposes the billionaire tax (Prop 40), they can simply vote no on 40 — they don't need Prop 42. Prop 42's main effect is a permanent constitutional ban on asset taxes, which limits future fiscal flexibility, and it's funded by billionaires with a self-interest. There's also the "poison pill"/deceptive ballot-box-gaming aspect. Meanwhile, the pro-side argument that middle-class retirement accounts are at risk is unsupported (no such proposal exists; Prop 40 explicitly excludes 401(k)s and pensions).

But wait: Prop 40 does include Roth IRAs over $10 million in "covered assets" per SF Chronicle. That's a partial merit to the pro argument, though very narrowly targeted.

Also worth considering: Does Prop 42's ban on retroactive taxes have legitimate merit? Some argue retroactive taxation is unfair; but the state commonly uses limited retroactivity (e.g., to Jan 1 of tax year) to prevent avoidance, and Prop 42 would bar that except for emergencies declared by the governor (only for legislative statutes, not ballot measures). That could hamper closing tax loopholes.

Now the decision. The question: "Is it better to vote yes or no on this prop?" I should weigh evidence and give a single answer. Most independent analyses and the majority of editorial boards (SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee/McClatchy, Mercury News/East Bay Times, LA Times columnist Skelton, League of Women Voters, California Democratic Party, California Budget & Policy Center) oppose it; it's overwhelmingly funded by self-interested billionaires (Brin >$100M across 41/42) with the explicit purpose of nullifying Prop 40; and it would constitutionally entrench a broad ban on taxing assets — removing future policy flexibility — while the claimed threat to middle-class retirement accounts is nonexistent (no proposals to tax 401(k)s; Prop 40 excludes them). Support from some unions (firefighters, building trades) is driven by their opposition to Prop 40, not by an actual threat to pensions.

Let me do a bit more research to confirm a few things:
1. League of Women Voters position on Prop 42 specifically.
2. Campaign finance totals for Prop 42 (how much from Brin).
3. Any counter-analysis arguing the ban has real value (e.g., that other states with wealth taxes saw out-migration; economists' views on wealth taxes).
4. Whether Prop 42 would apply to local taxes (no) and whether existing taxes are grandfathered (yes).

Also, I should check whether there's some significant legal argument that Prop 42 would be an unconstitutional attempt to bind future legislatures/voters (single-subject rule etc.), which could add uncertainty. Let me search a bit.

Let me do a couple more searches.

# Endorsement: Yes on Proposition 42
By The Times Editorial Board
May 18, 2014 12 AM PT
Should government workers and elected officials in cities, counties, water districts, school districts and other local governments be required to do their public business in public?
Should they be required to post meeting agendas and turn over documents on request?
Of course.
It’s a no-brainer.
We shouldn’t need a ballot measure to require them to obey what is already California law.
We shouldn’t have to go to the polls on June 3 to vote for Proposition 42.
We shouldn’t have to — but we do.
The Times strongly endorses Proposition 42.
The measure would amend the state Constitution to prevent lawmakers from suspending portions of the Ralph M. Brown Act requiring adequate public notice of local government meetings, and portions of the Public Records Act requiring that documents be available for public inspection.
Proposition 42 is necessary because the state’s budget crunch moved the governor and lawmakers to stop reimbursing cities, counties, schools and special districts for the costs of doing all that paperwork, and a few of those governments responded by threatening to simply stop doing it.
Without state money, they argued, open government laws were unfunded mandates and they didn’t have to comply.
Voters should make it clear that they do have to comply — government workers and politicians do have to obey

If you’ve seen the ads for it, Proposition 42 might seem like a common-sense measure.
Its opponents say it’s anything but.
The tag line for the yes on 42 campaign is “protect your retirement and life savings.” In the increasingly frequent ads for the measure, everyday people such as firefighters and teachers warn that state legislators have tried to tax such savings in the past, and the law is needed to safeguard everyone’s nest eggs.
But opponents of Prop. 42 say they see it as little more than a ruse to try to kill Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax. What’s worse, they say, is that because of the way the measure is written, it could harm much more than just that.
Here’s what Prop. 42 would do, why proponents think it’s needed, and why opponents say it’s a cynical and potentially dangerous measure.
What it would do: The measure would prohibit the state from imposing a wealth tax.
Specifically, it would bar any new taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026 that are placed on personal property; retirement or other kinds of personal savings; investments; business interests; and other non-real estate assets. It would also forbid any tax with retroactive provisions, such as to determine whether someone was a resident prior to the tax’s effective date, enacted after the start of this year.
Prop. 42 would nullify Prop. 40 — the billionaire tax (https://www.sfexaminer.com/news/politics/what-you-should-know-about-prop-40-the-billionaire-tax/article_e9e431c7-7577-43cf-b4fb-a0601b81c54c.html) — in the event that both pass but Prop. 42 attracts more votes.
When it would take effect: Five days after the Secretary of State certifies the election results — but it would apply to any applicable tax measures passed on or after Jan. 1 of this year.
Who would be covered by it: Ostensibly everyone in the state, but the only taxes on savings that are currently or have recently been considered are those on the wealthy — most notably, Prop. 40, which would only hit those with more than $1 billion in assets.
Who sponsored it: Reportedly, Sergey Brin (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/), the co-founder of Google, via Building a Better California (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/magazine/california-billionaires-tax.html), the political committee he formed earlier this year (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/27/us/politics/sergey-brin-gg-soto-trump-california-billionaire-tax.html).
Why: Opponents of Prop. 42 argue Brin and Building a Better California put it and Prop. 41 on the ballot specifically to stymie the billionaire tax. While ostensibly being about other things, both Prop. 41 and Prop. 42 include the same provision that would nullify Prop. 40 — even if it passes — should either one get more votes.
Reporting in The New York Times (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/magazine/california-billionaires-tax.html) and CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/) has backed up opponents’ assertions about that being the real motivation behind Prop. 42.
But earlier this year, Nathan Click, a spokesman for the yes on 42 campaign, denied that the measure was intended as a response to the billionaire-tax proposal. Instead, he said, Prop. 42 was designed to protect Californians’ retirement savings in the wake of efforts to tax them.
California’s Constitution allows such savings to be taxed, Prop. 42 proponents argue. In recent years, California legislators have proposed five different bills or constitutional amendments — not including Prop. 40 — that would have done just that, the campaign backing it points out on its website.
To be clear, all of those efforts, including Prop. 40, would have taxed wealthy residents; no one who had less than $15 million in assets would have had their retirement savings taxed under any of those measures, and all but one focused on those with at least $500 million in assets.
That said, Click said Prop. 42 was motivated by the fact that other tax policies in the past that were designed to be temporary or only hit richer people have been made permanent or extended to cover more of the populace.
Supporters: Building a Better California, the political committee that has gotten almost all of its funding from Brin and other billionaires (https://www.sfexaminer.com/news/politics/billionaire-tax-fight-has-become-200m-battle/article_31b8898d-bb5a-4ff5-97a0-5921537adea6.html). Politicians and political groups including Gov. Gavin Newsom and the California Republican Party. Business groups including the state and various local and ethnic chambers of commerce. Public-safety groups including the California Professional Firefighters and the California Association of Highway Patrolmen. Labor groups such as the State Building & Construction Trades Council and the California State Council of Laborers. Antitax groups such as the state and several local taxpayers associations.
Gov. Gavin Newsom (seen in San Francisco on Friday) has expressed opposition to Prop. 40 and support for Prop. 42.
Heather Diehl/Associated Press
Opponents: Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union that sponsored Prop. 40. Other labor groups, including the California Federation of Labor Unions, AFSCME California and United Teachers Los Angeles. Political groups including the California Democratic Party, California DSA and Working Families Party. Elected officials such as Rep. Ro Khanna, Assemblymember Alex Lee and U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont.
Rep. Ro Khanna of California, left, and U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, greet supporters during a campaign rally in support of California Proposition 40, known as the billionaire tax, and against propositions 41 and 42, in Los Angeles on Oct. 5.
Jae C. Hong/Associated Press
Arguments against it: Opponents say any arguments made in favor of Prop. 42 are just pretext.

If you’ve seen the ads for it, Proposition 42 might seem like a common-sense measure.
Its opponents say it’s anything but.
The tag line for the yes on 42 campaign is “protect your retirement and life savings.” In the increasingly frequent ads for the measure, everyday people such as firefighters and teachers warn that state legislators have tried to tax such savings in the past, and the law is needed to safeguard everyone’s nest eggs.
But opponents of Prop. 42 say they see it as little more than a ruse to try to kill Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax. What’s worse, they say, is that because of the way the measure is written, it could harm much more than just that.
Here’s what Prop. 42 would do, why proponents think it’s needed, and why opponents say it’s a cynical and potentially dangerous measure.
What it would do: The measure would prohibit the state from imposing a wealth tax.
Specifically, it would bar any new taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026 that are placed on personal property; retirement or other kinds of personal savings; investments; business interests; and other non-real estate assets. It would also forbid any tax with retroactive provisions, such as to determine whether someone was a resident prior to the tax’s effective date, enacted after the start of this year.
Prop. 42 would nullify Prop. 40 — the billionaire tax (https://www.sfexaminer.com/news/politics/what-you-should-know-about-prop-40-the-billionaire-tax/article_e9e431c7-7577-43cf-b4fb-a0601b81c54c.html) — in the event that both pass but Prop. 42 attracts more votes.
When it would take effect: Five days after the Secretary of State certifies the election results — but it would apply to any applicable tax measures passed on or after Jan. 1 of this year.
Who would be covered by it: Ostensibly everyone in the state, but the only taxes on savings that are currently or have recently been considered are those on the wealthy — most notably, Prop. 40, which would only hit those with more than $1 billion in assets.
Who sponsored it: Reportedly, Sergey Brin (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/), the co-founder of Google, via Building a Better California (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/magazine/california-billionaires-tax.html), the political committee he formed earlier this year (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/27/us/politics/sergey-brin-gg-soto-trump-california-billionaire-tax.html).
Why: Opponents of Prop. 42 argue Brin and Building a Better California put it and Prop. 41 on the ballot specifically to stymie the billionaire tax. While ostensibly being about other things, both Prop. 41 and Prop. 42 include the same provision that would nullify Prop. 40 — even if it passes — should either one get more votes.
Reporting in The New York Times (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/magazine/california-billionaires-tax.html) and CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/) has backed up opponents’ assertions about that being the real motivation behind Prop. 42.
But earlier this year, Nathan Click, a spokesman for the yes on 42 campaign, denied that the measure was intended as a response to the billionaire-tax proposal. Instead, he said, Prop. 42 was designed to protect Californians’ retirement savings in the wake of efforts to tax them.
California’s Constitution allows such savings to be taxed, Prop. 42 proponents argue. In recent years, California legislators have proposed five different bills or constitutional amendments — not including Prop. 40 — that would have done just that, the campaign backing it points out on its website.
To be clear, all of those efforts, including Prop. 40, would have taxed wealthy residents; no one who had less than $15 million in assets would have had their retirement savings taxed under any of those measures, and all but one focused on those with at least $500 million in assets.
That said, Click said Prop. 42 was motivated by the fact that other tax policies in the past that were designed to be temporary or only hit richer people have been made permanent or extended to cover more of the populace.
